opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the PUCT rule comes out of AlphaGo and AlphaZero. At each node you pick the child that maximizes Q plus an exploration bonus: a constant times the prior probability of that action, times the square root of the parent's visit count, divided by one plus the child's visit count. That's a really elegant heuristic for Go or chess, where you have a few hundred legal moves, you can afford thousands of simulations per move, and the visit counts actually grow large enough for that square-root term to do its job.

With language models, almost every one of those assumptions breaks. First, the branching factor is enormous. If your actions are tokens, you've got a vocabulary of a hundred thousand or more. If your actions are sentences or reasoning steps, the space is effectively infinite, so you're sampling children rather than enumerating them. The prior gets spread incredibly thin, and most children will only ever be visited once or zero times. The exploration bonus basically never gets the repeated visits it needs to balance against Q. You end up in a regime where the formula is dominated by noise in the prior and your first few value estimates.

Second, a lot of those branches are semantically the same thing. Two different token sequences can express the identical idea, and PUCT treats them as completely distinct arms. So you can waste your whole budget "exploring" what is really one path written ten different ways, while never trying a genuinely different approach.

Third, it's just expensive. In Go, a forward pass of the network is cheap relative to the game, and the tree is shallow enough that the statistics propagate. In LLM reasoning, every expansion might be hundreds of tokens, and the value signal often only shows up at the very end, like whether the proof checked out or the code passed the tests. So your Q estimates are sparse and high variance, and the constant c that balances exploration and exploitation becomes this very finicky hyperparameter that doesn't transfer across problems.

So I think the core intuition, spending compute on promising branches while still hedging, is right. But the specific PUCT formula is tuned for small, discrete, enumerable action spaces with dense simulation. For LLMs you probably want exploration defined over something more like distinct ideas or plans, with diversity measured semantically, rather than per-token visit counts.

r001.rationale: The response says that most children will be visited only once or zero times, directly conveying that repeated sampling of the same child is unlikely.

r002.rationale: It describes token actions as having a huge vocabulary and sentence or reasoning-step actions as effectively infinite, requiring sampling rather than enumeration. It says this makes PUCT’s discrete, enumerable action-space assumptions a poor fit.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing to remember about PUCT is where it came from. It was designed for Go and chess, for a very specific regime: a fixed, fairly small branching factor, a cheap simulator, and a policy prior that's roughly calibrated because you trained it on exactly the states you're going to search over. In that world the formula does something elegant. You've got the Q term, the value estimate, and then the exploration bonus that scales with the prior times the square root of parent visits over one plus child visits. You run tens of thousands of simulations, the visit counts converge, and the whole thing behaves like a nice regret-minimizing bandit at each node.

Almost none of those assumptions hold when the nodes are LLM reasoning steps.

The first problem is the branching factor. In Go you have at most 361 actions and you enumerate all of them. With a language model, the action space is effectively infinite. You're sampling candidate continuations, maybe four, maybe eight, and those samples are themselves the exploration. So the question CPUCT is designed to answer, "which of these fully enumerated children should I visit next," is kind of the wrong question. The real question is "should I sample a new child at all, and if so, what temperature." PUCT has no notion of an unexpanded action that you haven't even seen yet. People bolt on progressive widening, but at that point you're fighting the formula rather than using it.

Second, the prior is miscalibrated in a way that the formula is really sensitive to. In AlphaZero, the policy network's probability over moves is a direct estimate of how often the search ended up choosing that move. With an LLM, the "prior" you'd plug in is the sequence log-probability of a chunk of text, and that number is dominated by things that have nothing to do with correctness. Longer continuations get lower probability. Boilerplate phrasing gets higher probability. A correct but unusually worded step can be 20 nats less likely than a confident, fluent, wrong one. So the exploration bonus ends up rewarding fluency instead of promise. And because the prior multiplies the bonus, a mis-estimate doesn't average out, it compounds over the whole subtree.

Third, and I think this is the deepest one, is the compute asymmetry. The C in CPUCT is tuned under the assumption that simulations are cheap and plentiful. The square root of parent visits term only means anything once N is in the hundreds or thousands. With an LLM, each expansion is a forward pass, maybe a few hundred tokens, and each value estimate is possibly another forward pass. You might get a total budget of fifty or a hundred node expansions for an entire problem. In that regime the visit counts never get large enough for the UCB-style confidence bound to be meaningful. You're essentially in the first few iterations of the bandit forever, where the exploration term is just noise shaped by the prior.

And there's a related thing about what the value signal looks like. In games you get a crisp terminal reward. For reasoning you usually have a learned verifier or a process reward model that's noisy and often systematically overconfident on exactly the kind of plausible-looking garbage the LLM likes to produce. PUCT averages Q over backups, which is fine when the noise is zero-mean, but verifier errors are correlated along a path. If the model has convinced itself of a false lemma, every downstream step will look good to the verifier too. So the Q estimates along that branch all go up together, and the exploration term is too weak to pull you out.

What I think works better is to stop treating it as a bandit over a tree and start treating it more like a beam or a best-first search with some diversity pressure. Something like: score partial trajectories with your verifier, keep a frontier, and explicitly penalize siblings that are semantically similar rather than relying on visit counts to spread things out. Or honestly, in a lot of cases, just do parallel sampling with a good verifier and skip the tree altogether. The tree structure in Go is load-bearing because the game has real alternation and real adversarial branching. In a lot of LLM reasoning there's no opponent, so a lot of the machinery MCTS carries around is dead weight.

I'd put it this way. CPUCT is a great answer to the question "how do I allocate a million cheap rollouts over a known action set with a calibrated prior." LLM search is a hundred expensive rollouts over an open action set with a prior that mostly measures fluency. You can make the formula run, but you're using the wrong tool and then tuning the constant to compensate.

r001.rationale: The response says continuations are sampled and discusses unexpanded actions, but does not state that LLM tree search is unlikely to sample the same child more than once.

r002.rationale: It describes the LLM action space as effectively infinite and argues that choosing among fully enumerated children is the wrong model because new continuations must be sampled.

astra-6.text:
The issue is that PUCT is designed around a setting where you can visit the same node many times. You have a relatively small set of actions, and you keep trading off between exploiting the action with the highest estimated value and exploring actions you’re less certain about.

With language models, you have this enormous action space, and generating a branch is expensive. If your actions are whole reasoning steps, you may never sample the same action twice. So you’re in a regime where the assumptions behind those visit counts don’t fit very well. You can spend your entire search budget just beginning to explore the tree.

There’s also the question of what the policy prior means. A language model assigning high probability to a continuation doesn’t necessarily mean that continuation is a promising way to solve the problem. It might just mean it’s a conventional way to phrase the next sentence. PUCT uses that prior to allocate exploration, so it can keep directing compute toward very similar, plausible-looking approaches.

What you really want is to spend compute on meaningfully different hypotheses, and then use the results to decide what to try next. You can adapt tree search to do that, but I don’t think taking the exploration rule from a board-game setting and applying it directly to language is necessarily the right allocation of compute.

r001.rationale: The response says that when actions are whole reasoning steps, search may never sample the same action twice.

r002.rationale: It contrasts PUCT’s relatively small action set with language models’ enormous action space and says those visit-count assumptions do not fit well.

sol-6.1.text:
The issue is that PUCT allocates exploration according to the policy’s prior probability. That’s a reasonable heuristic when you have a fairly small action space and a policy that’s already good at identifying promising moves. But for language, the probability of a continuation isn’t necessarily a good measure of how useful it is for solving the problem.

You might have a hundred different ways of expressing essentially the same idea, and then one low-probability continuation that actually changes the approach. The search can spend its budget exploring those hundred paraphrases instead of discovering the new approach. And if your actions are entire reasoning steps, their probabilities also depend on length and wording in ways that have little to do with their value.

So the exploration bonus is measuring something different from what you really care about. You want to explore distinct hypotheses, or places where another sample could change your assessment. Token probability doesn’t directly tell you either of those things. PUCT can still be a useful baseline, but I wouldn’t assume the exploration rule that worked for Go is the right one for reasoning in language.

r001.rationale: The response discusses spending search budget on paraphrases, but does not state that LLM tree search is unlikely to sample the same child more than once.

r002.rationale: It notes many ways to express an idea and that language probabilities can mislead, but does not argue that language’s open-ended action space makes modeling actions as a discrete set inappropriate.
